## Learning Objectives

After completing this chapter, you will be able to:

1. Explain how Excel-based audit analytics supports risk assessment, substantive testing, and internal control evaluation in professional practice.
2. Apply stratification techniques to segment a transaction population by size and characteristic and use the results to guide audit sampling decisions.
3. Perform a Benford's Law analysis on accounting transaction data to identify digit frequency patterns that deviate from expected distributions.
4. Build an aging analysis for receivables that classifies outstanding balances into time-based categories and supports estimation of the allowance for doubtful accounts.
5. Use Excel formulas and conditional logic to detect duplicate transactions, identify sequence gaps, and flag journal entries that exhibit characteristics associated with control override.
6. Document Excel-based audit analytics in a workpaper format that meets professional standards for completeness, clarity, and reviewability.

---

## Opening Scenario

You are an internal auditor at Charles River, and the audit manager has assigned you to the quarterly review of journal entries and payment transactions. Your responsibilities include testing whether vendor payment amounts follow expected statistical patterns, determining whether any duplicate payments were processed during the quarter, evaluating the aging of outstanding customer receivables, and reviewing journal entries for indicators of control override such as entries posted on weekends, entries with round-dollar amounts, and entries recorded just below management approval thresholds. The data you need comes from three areas of the company's system. The DisbursementPayment table in the Procure-to-Pay group records every payment to a supplier. The SalesInvoice table in the Order-to-Cash group records every customer billing and its due date. The JournalEntry and GLEntry tables in the Accounting Core record the manual entries and the posted ledger detail that ultimately support the financial statements. All of this data is available to you as the Charles River Excel workbook. The audit manager expects you to deliver your findings in a set of organized workpapers that document each test, its results, and your conclusions. This chapter teaches you the Excel techniques that support every step of that assignment.

---

## Audit Analytics and the Role of Excel

The previous four chapters introduced Excel as a tool for organizing data, cleaning and preparing it, summarizing it through descriptive analytics, and building analytical models. This chapter applies those same Excel capabilities to a different purpose. Instead of describing business performance or projecting future outcomes, the techniques here focus on testing the integrity of accounting data, identifying anomalies that may indicate errors or fraud, and evaluating whether internal controls operated effectively during the period under review.

Audit analytics refers to the use of data analysis techniques to examine entire populations of accounting transactions rather than relying exclusively on manual inspection of selected samples. The concept is not new. Vasarhelyi and Halper (1991) proposed continuous auditing as a way to use technology for ongoing monitoring of financial data, and their framework anticipated many of the techniques that auditors now apply routinely using spreadsheet and database tools. What has changed is the accessibility of the tools. Excel provides functions for stratification, statistical analysis, text matching, date calculations, and conditional logic that together support a comprehensive set of audit tests. The AICPA's Guide to Audit Data Analytics (2017) identified Excel as one of the primary tools auditors use for data analytics, noting that its widespread availability and its familiarity to accounting professionals make it a practical starting point for audit analytics programs.

The professional standards that govern auditing support and in some cases require the use of analytical techniques. AU-C Section 520, Analytical Procedures (AICPA, 2020), requires auditors to perform analytical procedures during the risk assessment phase and during the overall review of financial statements. AS 2305 of the PCAOB standards similarly requires the use of analytical procedures as substantive tests when they can provide appropriate evidence. Analytical procedures include comparisons of recorded amounts to expectations developed by the auditor, and the precision of those expectations depends on the quality of the data and the rigor of the analytical technique. The techniques in this chapter, including stratification, digital analysis, aging, and anomaly detection, are all forms of analytical procedures or tools that support the design of more effective procedures.

This chapter draws on three Charles River table groups, each chosen because it represents a population that auditors test in practice. The Procure-to-Pay group supplies the DisbursementPayment table, which records every supplier payment with its amount, payment date, and supplier reference, making it the natural population for digital analysis and duplicate detection. The Order-to-Cash group supplies the SalesInvoice table, which records customer billings along with an invoice date and a due date, making it the natural population for aging analysis. The Accounting Core supplies the JournalEntry and GLEntry tables, which together capture every manual entry and every posted debit and credit in the company. Because every business cycle in Charles River ultimately posts to GLEntry, the Accounting Core serves as the integration point where revenue, expense, and adjustment activity can all be tested for control override. Working with these three groups gives you exposure to the receivable, payable, and ledger populations that anchor most audit analytics work.

*[Figure 8.1: Audit Analytics Workflow in Excel. A horizontal flow diagram showing five stages: Data Acquisition (importing Charles River data into Excel), Population Profiling (stratification and descriptive statistics), Analytical Testing (Benford's Law, aging, ratio analysis), Anomaly Investigation (duplicate detection, journal entry testing), and Documentation (workpaper preparation). Each stage shows the Excel techniques used and connects to the next with an arrow.]*

> **[CONNECTING THE DOTS]**

Benford's Law analysis uses the LEFT and TEXT functions from Chapter 5 and the COUNTIF function from Chapter 6. Aging analysis uses date arithmetic and IF functions from Chapter 4. This chapter applies familiar tools to a new professional context rather than introducing entirely new technical capabilities.

## Stratification of Account Balances

Stratification is the process of dividing a population of transactions or balances into subgroups based on a characteristic such as dollar amount, account type, or transaction date. In audit work, stratification serves two purposes. First, it provides the auditor with a profile of the population that reveals how transactions are distributed across size categories, which helps the auditor identify where the largest concentrations of dollar value exist. Second, it supports the design of a sampling strategy by allowing the auditor to select samples from different strata in proportion to their risk or their dollar contribution to the total.

The concept is straightforward. Suppose you have a population of supplier payments ranging from a few dollars to several hundred thousand dollars. A stratification table might divide this population into five bands such as payments under 1,000 dollars, payments from 1,000 to 9,999 dollars, payments from 10,000 to 49,999 dollars, payments from 50,000 to 99,999 dollars, and payments of 100,000 dollars or more. For each band, the table reports the count of transactions, the total dollar value, and the percentage of the total population and total value represented by that band. The result is a compact summary that tells the auditor, for example, that most payments are small but represent only a fraction of the total dollar value, while a handful of large payments represent the majority of the dollars at risk. That information directly affects how the auditor allocates testing effort.

Auditing standards recognize the value of stratification. ISA 530, Audit Sampling (IAASB, 2009), states that stratification can increase the efficiency of audit sampling by allowing the auditor to direct testing effort toward the items that are most significant or most likely to contain misstatements. The AICPA's Guide to Audit Data Analytics (2017) describes stratification as one of the foundational data analytics techniques for auditors, applicable to both substantive testing and tests of controls.

Stratification also shapes the sampling method the auditor selects. When a population is dominated by a small number of large items, the auditor often examines every item in the top stratum, because those items carry enough individual dollar value that a single misstatement could be material, and then samples from the lower strata where the risk is spread across many smaller transactions. This approach is the foundation of monetary unit sampling, a method in which the probability that an item is selected is proportional to its dollar value. The stratification table makes the logic visible, because once the auditor can see that a handful of payments represent the majority of the dollars, the decision to test those payments in full follows naturally. The AICPA's Guide to Audit Data Analytics (2017) describes this profiling step as a precondition for an efficient sampling design, since an auditor who understands the shape of the population before sampling can direct effort where the dollar risk actually concentrates.

In Excel, stratification can be accomplished using COUNTIFS and SUMIFS with boundary conditions, or by using PivotTables with grouped value ranges. The formula approach gives you precise control over the boundaries, while the PivotTable approach is faster for exploration. Both approaches produce the same result, and the choice depends on whether you need a permanent, documented analysis, where formulas are preferable because they are transparent and auditable, or a quick preliminary look at the data, where PivotTables are more efficient.

## Benford's Law Analysis

Benford's Law, also known as the first-digit law, describes the expected frequency distribution of leading digits in many naturally occurring datasets. The law states that the digit 1 should appear as the leading digit approximately 30.1 percent of the time, the digit 2 approximately 17.6 percent, and so on, with the digit 9 appearing as the leading digit only about 4.6 percent of the time. This pattern was first observed by the astronomer Simon Newcomb in 1881 and later formalized by the physicist Frank Benford in 1938, who demonstrated that the pattern held across data from diverse sources including population figures, street addresses, and river drainage areas.

The mathematical basis for Benford's Law is the logarithmic distribution of significant digits. The probability that the first digit is d is given by the formula P(d) = log10(1 + 1/d) for d = 1, 2, through 9. This distribution arises naturally in datasets that span several orders of magnitude and that result from multiplicative processes or from the combination of data from multiple sources. Accounting data frequently exhibits these characteristics. Payment amounts, invoice totals, journal entry amounts, and account balances typically range from small to very large values and are generated by many different transactions and processes.

Nigrini (1996) demonstrated the application of Benford's Law to accounting and auditing data and showed that deviations from the expected distribution can indicate data anomalies that warrant investigation. His work established digital analysis as a practical audit tool. Subsequent research has confirmed the usefulness of Benford's Law in audit settings. Durtschi, Hillison, and Pacini (2004) provided guidance on when Benford's Law is and is not appropriate, noting that it works well for datasets such as accounts payable, accounts receivable, and general ledger balances, but may not apply to datasets with imposed minimums or maximums, such as reimbursement amounts capped at a policy limit, or to datasets where values are assigned rather than naturally generated, such as check numbers or invoice numbers.

> **[WATCH OUT]**
> Benford's Law does not apply to every dataset. It works best with data that spans multiple orders of magnitude and is not constrained by minimums, maximums, or assigned ranges. Datasets composed of telephone numbers, identification numbers, or randomly generated values will not follow Benford's distribution. Before performing a Benford's Law analysis, confirm that the dataset has the characteristics that make the analysis meaningful. If a dataset contains only values between 100 and 999 dollars, the leading digit distribution will not follow Benford's Law because the values do not span enough orders of magnitude.

In audit practice, a Benford's Law analysis does not prove that fraud or error exists. It identifies deviations from the expected pattern that may justify further investigation. A higher-than-expected frequency of leading digit 5, for example, might indicate nothing more than a coincidental clustering of payment amounts in the 5,000 dollar range. Alternatively, it might indicate that someone is creating payments at amounts just below a review threshold. The analysis raises the question, and the auditor's professional judgment determines the answer.

*[Figure 8.3: Benford's Law Expected Distribution. A bar chart showing the expected frequency of each leading digit (1 through 9) according to Benford's Law. The tallest bar is digit 1 at 30.1 percent, declining to digit 9 at 4.6 percent. The chart uses a clean, professional style with labeled bars.]*

## Aging Analysis

An aging analysis classifies outstanding balances by the length of time they have been outstanding, typically using time bands such as current, 1 to 30 days past due, 31 to 60 days past due, 61 to 90 days past due, and over 90 days past due. Aging analysis is one of the most widely used analytical procedures in accounting because it serves multiple purposes across the three accounting perspectives. In financial accounting, the aging schedule supports the estimation of the allowance for doubtful accounts under the current expected credit loss model, as required by ASC 326 (FASB, 2016). In managerial accounting, the aging schedule provides visibility into collection performance and working capital management. In auditing, the aging schedule serves as the basis for evaluating management's estimate of uncollectible accounts and for selecting balances for confirmation procedures.

The mechanics of aging analysis in Excel depend on calculating the number of days between a reference date, typically the reporting date, and the date that determines when the balance became due, and then classifying each transaction into the appropriate time band using nested IF formulas or lookup logic. Charles River supports this analysis directly because the SalesInvoice table records both an InvoiceDate and a DueDate for every customer invoice. Subtracting the DueDate from the reporting date produces the number of days past due, and a nested IF formula then assigns each invoice to a category based on that number.

## Duplicate Detection and Gap Analysis

Duplicate transactions are one of the most common anomalies auditors test for in accounting data. A duplicate payment, for example, occurs when the same supplier is paid twice for the same invoice. Duplicates can arise from data entry errors, system glitches, or, in some cases, deliberate manipulation. Detecting duplicates requires comparing records across multiple fields to identify matches that suggest a payment was processed more than once.

In Excel, duplicate detection relies on building a composite key from the fields that together should uniquely identify a transaction, and then testing whether that composite key appears more than once in the dataset. For the Charles River supplier payments, the relevant fields are the supplier reference, the payment amount, and the payment date. For journal entries, the relevant fields might include the posting date, the account, and the amount.

The COUNTIFS function is the primary tool for duplicate detection. The formula counts how many records in the dataset share the same values across all the specified fields. If the count exceeds one, the record is flagged as a potential duplicate. A helper column containing the COUNTIFS result makes it easy to filter for and review the flagged items. Applied to the DisbursementPayment table, the formula =COUNTIFS(DisbursementPayment[SupplierID], [@SupplierID], DisbursementPayment[Amount], [@Amount], DisbursementPayment[PaymentDate], [@PaymentDate]) counts how many payments share the same supplier, amount, and date as the current row.

An alternative approach creates a composite key by concatenating the relevant fields into a single text string using the CONCAT function or the ampersand operator. For example, =[@SupplierID]&"-"&TEXT([@Amount], "0.00")&"-"&TEXT([@PaymentDate], "YYYY-MM-DD") creates a unique string that combines supplier, amount, and date. You can then use COUNTIF on the composite key column to count occurrences. Any value greater than one indicates a potential duplicate.

A flagged duplicate is a starting point for investigation, not a confirmed error. Two payments to the same supplier for the same amount on the same date may be a genuine double payment, or they may be two legitimate settlements of two separate invoices that happened to carry identical amounts. Before concluding that a payment was duplicated, the auditor examines the supporting records, which in the Charles River data means tracing each flagged DisbursementPayment back to its PurchaseInvoiceID to confirm whether the two payments settled the same invoice or two different ones. This discipline of reviewing before concluding mirrors the principle introduced in Chapter 5, where potential duplicates in a dataset are flagged for review rather than removed automatically, because deleting records without documentation would compromise the completeness of the population and the reliability of the audit conclusion.

*[Figure 8.9: Example of a COUNTIFS-based duplicate detection formula applied to Charles River DisbursementPayment data, with a filter showing flagged records where the count exceeds 1. The matching fields are SupplierID, Amount, and PaymentDate. Annotations explain the formula and the interpretation.]*

### Gap Analysis

Gap analysis tests the completeness of a sequence of numbers, such as check numbers, invoice numbers, or journal entry numbers. Accounting systems typically assign sequential numbers to transactions, and gaps in the sequence may indicate missing or deleted transactions. In audit work, sequence testing is a standard procedure for evaluating the completeness assertion.

The Charles River SalesInvoice table assigns each invoice an InvoiceNumber. To perform gap analysis in Excel, isolate the numeric portion of the invoice number if it carries a document-type prefix, sort the data by that number, and then create a column that calculates the difference between each record's number and the previous record's number. The formula =[@InvoiceNum] - A2, which references the cell directly above, calculates the gap. Any result other than 1 indicates a gap in the sequence. You can then filter for gaps greater than 1 to identify the missing numbers.

*[Figure 8.10: Gap analysis on a sequence of Charles River sales invoice numbers. A helper column shows the difference between consecutive invoice numbers. Rows where the gap exceeds 1 are highlighted with conditional formatting, indicating potentially missing invoice numbers.]*

> **[IN PRACTICE]**
> Auditors test invoice number and check number sequences as part of their evaluation of the completeness of recorded transactions. A gap in the invoice number sequence, for example, might indicate a voided invoice that was not properly recorded. Auditors investigate each gap to determine whether the missing numbers were voided, were part of a test batch, or represent transactions that were improperly removed from the records.

## Journal Entry Testing for Control Override

One of the most important applications of audit analytics is testing journal entries for characteristics associated with management override of internal controls. Fraudulent financial reporting often involves manipulating journal entries to inflate revenue, reduce expenses, or shift costs between periods. The auditing standards address this risk directly. AS 2401 of the PCAOB standards and ISA 240 (IAASB, 2009) require auditors to test journal entries as part of their response to the risk of management override of controls.

In the Charles River database, the JournalEntry table stores the headers for manually created entries, including the PostingDate, the EntryType, and the employee who approved the entry, while the GLEntry table stores the posted debit and credit detail. Because manual journal entries are the mechanism most often used to override controls, the JournalEntry and GLEntry tables together form the population for this testing. The characteristics that auditors look for include entries posted on weekends or holidays when the accounting department is normally closed, entries with unusually round dollar amounts that may indicate estimation rather than actual transaction recording, entries posted just below authorization thresholds to avoid review and approval, entries made by individuals who do not normally make journal entries, and entries posted to unusual account combinations such as a debit to revenue and a credit to an expense account.

In Excel, each of these tests translates into a formula or conditional expression that flags entries meeting the specified criteria.

For weekend testing, the WEEKDAY function returns a number from 1 to 7 for any date. Applied to the GLEntry PostingDate, the formula =IF(OR(WEEKDAY([@PostingDate], 2)=6, WEEKDAY([@PostingDate], 2)=7), "Weekend", "Weekday") flags entries posted on Saturday or Sunday. The second argument of 2 in the WEEKDAY function specifies that the week starts on Monday, which makes Saturday equal to 6 and Sunday equal to 7.

For round-amount testing, the MOD function tests whether an amount is divisible by a round number. Applied to the Debit column, the formula =IF(MOD([@Debit], 1000)=0, "Round (1000s)", IF(MOD([@Debit], 100)=0, "Round (100s)", "Not Round")) identifies entries where the amount is exactly divisible by 1,000 or 100. The auditor defines the threshold for what constitutes a round amount based on the context and the materiality of the engagement.

For threshold testing, a simple comparison identifies entries that fall just below a known approval limit. If the approval threshold is 10,000 dollars, the formula =IF(AND([@Debit]>=9000, [@Debit]<10000), "Below Threshold", "") flags entries in the range from 9,000 to 9,999.99 dollars. The auditor adjusts the lower bound of the range based on professional judgment about what constitutes just below the threshold.

*[Figure 8.11: Journal entry testing formulas applied to Charles River GLEntry data. Three helper columns show the results of the weekend test, the round-amount test, and the threshold test. Entries that are flagged on multiple criteria are highlighted.]*

> **[WATCH OUT]**
> Journal entry testing produces flags, not conclusions. A journal entry posted on a Sunday is not necessarily fraudulent. The company may have batch processing that runs on weekends, or an accountant may have worked overtime to meet a deadline. Similarly, a round-dollar amount may reflect a legitimate accrual or estimate rather than a fabricated entry. Many recurring entries in Charles River, such as monthly rent and depreciation, post on fixed calendar days and carry round amounts for legitimate reasons. The purpose of these tests is to identify entries that warrant investigation, not to make accusations. The auditor's professional judgment determines whether a flagged entry requires follow-up, and the follow-up consists of examining supporting documentation and discussing the entry with management.

### Combining Multiple Flags

In practice, auditors are most interested in journal entries that exhibit more than one unusual characteristic simultaneously. An entry that was posted on a weekend, involves a round dollar amount, and falls just below the approval threshold is more suspicious than an entry that exhibits only one of these characteristics. In Excel, you can create a composite risk score by adding the individual flag columns together. Assign a value of 1 to each flag, so that a weekend posting equals 1, a round amount equals 1, and a near-threshold amount equals 1, and sum them in a RiskScore column. Entries with a risk score of 2 or higher deserve priority attention.

*[Figure 8.12: A RiskScore column that sums three binary flag columns (Weekend, RoundAmount, NearThreshold) for Charles River journal entries. The data is sorted by RiskScore in descending order, with the highest-risk entries at the top. Conditional formatting applies red highlighting to entries with a score of 2 or more.]*

> **[CONNECTING THE DOTS]**
> In Chapter 12, you will build these same journal entry tests using SQL queries against the Charles River GLEntry and JournalEntry tables. The SQL approach allows you to combine multiple tests into a single query using CASE expressions and to save the query as a reusable template for future engagements. In Chapter 19, the journal entry testing framework is extended with additional tests for forensic accounting investigations, including analysis of entries that move amounts between revenue and expense accounts and detection of entries posted near the period-end close.

## Ratio Analysis and Trend Comparison for Analytical Procedures

Ratio analysis and trend comparison are foundational analytical procedures that auditors use to set expectations for account balances and to identify balances that may be misstated. While these techniques were introduced conceptually in earlier chapters, this section focuses specifically on how auditors use them as part of a structured analytical procedure.

An analytical procedure, as defined in AU-C Section 520 (AICPA, 2020), consists of four steps. The auditor develops an expectation for the amount or ratio being tested. The auditor determines the threshold for investigation, which is the amount of difference between the expectation and the recorded balance that would require further inquiry. The auditor compares the recorded amount to the expectation. And the auditor investigates differences that exceed the threshold.

In Excel, these steps translate into a structured worksheet. A common approach is to build a table with columns for the account or ratio name, the current period recorded balance, the expectation, which may come from a prior period balance, a budgeted amount, a regression prediction, or an industry benchmark, the difference, the percentage difference, the threshold, and a flag indicating whether the difference exceeds the threshold. In Charles River, the current period balances come from summing the Debit and Credit columns of GLEntry by account, and budget expectations come from the Budget table in the Organizational Planning group, which records a BudgetAmount for each account and cost center by fiscal period.

The expectation can be derived from several sources. Trend analysis uses the prior period balance adjusted for known changes such as revenue growth or a new product launch. Ratio analysis compares the current period ratio, such as gross margin or days sales outstanding, to the prior period ratio or to an industry benchmark. Regression analysis, covered in Chapter 7, uses a statistical model to generate the expectation. The choice of method depends on the precision required by the circumstances of the engagement.

*[Figure 8.13: An analytical procedures worksheet showing account names, current balances drawn from GLEntry, expectations derived from prior year balances adjusted for growth, differences, percentage differences, thresholds, and investigation flags. Accounts where the percentage difference exceeds the threshold are highlighted.]*

> **[IN PRACTICE]**
> Auditors are required to document their analytical procedures in workpapers that show the expectation, the threshold, the comparison, and the conclusion for each account tested. The worksheet format shown in Figure 8.13 is a common workpaper template used in practice. The precision of the expectation, which is influenced by the analytical method used and the reliability of the underlying data, directly affects the persuasiveness of the audit evidence obtained. A regression-based expectation from independently sourced data provides stronger evidence than a simple trend comparison based on the client's own prior period data.

## Documenting Excel-Based Audit Analytics

Every analytical test performed in Excel should be documented in a format that allows another auditor to understand what was done, why it was done, how it was done, and what conclusions were reached. Documentation is not an afterthought added after the analysis is complete. It is a professional requirement and a quality control mechanism.

The PCAOB's AS 1215, Audit Documentation, requires that audit documentation be sufficient to enable an experienced auditor with no prior connection to the engagement to understand the nature, timing, extent, and results of the procedures performed, the evidence obtained, and the conclusions reached. For Excel-based analytics, this standard means that each workbook should contain enough information for a reviewer to replicate the analysis independently.

A well-documented audit analytics workbook follows a consistent structure. The first worksheet is an index or table of contents that lists all worksheets in the workbook and describes their contents. The second worksheet contains the raw data as imported from the source system, with a note identifying the source, the date of extraction, and the number of records. Subsequent worksheets contain the individual analytical tests, each with a clear title, a description of the test objective, the formulas or procedures applied, and the results. The final worksheet contains a summary of findings that identifies the anomalies detected, the follow-up actions taken or recommended, and the overall conclusion.

Each analytical test worksheet should include several elements. A header section contains the test name, the dataset used, the date performed, and the preparer's name. A description section explains the objective of the test in one or two sentences. The analysis section contains the data, formulas, and results. A conclusion section states the finding in clear, professional language and notes whether the result is consistent with expectations or whether it requires follow-up.

*[Figure 8.14: Example of a well-documented audit analytics worksheet in Excel. The header section shows the test name, "Benford's Law Analysis of Supplier Payments," the dataset, "Charles River DisbursementPayment, Q3," the date, and the preparer. The description states the test objective. The analysis area shows the digit frequency comparison table and chart. The conclusion section summarizes the findings and identifies digits requiring follow-up.]*

> **[IN PRACTICE]**
> Audit firms often establish templates for Excel-based analytics workpapers that enforce consistent documentation standards. Staff auditors populate the templates with the data and analysis, and senior team members review the workpapers for completeness and accuracy. The documentation standard applies regardless of whether the analysis is performed in Excel, SQL, or specialized audit software. The principle is the same across all tools, that another qualified professional should be able to pick up the workpaper and understand what was done without asking the preparer for explanations.
